utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let me first of all apologise to everyone for the late start this afternoon caused by the cancellation of my flight back here, which I regret was unavoidable. We will, as a result, sit from now until 5.00, and then from 5.30 until 7.00. Good afternoon, Mr. Shaqiri.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you now make the solemn declaration, please, by reading aloud the document which will be placed before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please be seated. Just one thing I'd like to say to you before your evidence starts, Mr. Shaqiri. We've been experiencing some difficulty in the presentation of evidence here because witnesses often want to give an account of things that are not necessarily the things that the Tribunal and the lawyers here are most interested in. So it's very important if your evidence is to have its maximum impact that you pay very close attention to the questions that are asked and confine the answer you give to the point that the question deals with. I hope you understand what I'm saying, that we want to concentrate on -- we want to concentrate on the issues that the parties here consider to be the important ones. And to enable us to cover as many of these as possible, it's vital that the answers given are directed to the point that's asked about. So with that introduction we'll move straight to the questions, and the first counsel to ask questions of you will be for the Prosecution, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would indicate for the record that this is a viva voce witness, that his testimony, Your Honour, relates to paragraphs 72(i) and 73 of the indictment relating to deportation and forced transfers, relating to Gnjilane or Gjilan municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sir, could you state our first and last name and spell it for the court reporter?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: My name is Abdylhaqim Shaqiri.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And, sir, I just want to recite some biographical data and will you advise me whether or not this is correct. You are a Kosovo Albanian, born in Prilepnica village in Gjilan municipality in Kosovo in 1949?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And, sir, I understand you've lived there most all your life up until 1999; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand further that you're married with four children, two sons and two daughters?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And could you tell the Court what your current job or occupation is.

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: I am an imam in Prilepnica mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how long have you been the imam there?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: From 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I understand that that's somewhat of a family tradition in your family; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Yes, we have this for generations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your father and grandfather were both imams in that area?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Yes, they've been imams from the time of Turkey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sir, what area did you cover as imam? Was it just the village of Prilepnica?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Part of the village of Prilepnica there is Kmetofc, Verbica village covered by this mosque, another village Kosaca, and the people who live in Poropotova, part of Prilepnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Briefly could you describe what are your duties as imam in that area?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: We carry out religious duties as imams. We perform our duty in the mosque during the prayer, and then when someone dies we escort the coffin to the cemetery. We teach students who come to the mosque. We perform the marriage ritual and baptise the newly born and other religious rites as we are asked for by the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, when you were a young man in Kosovo, did you have to perform military duty, mandatory military service?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When did you do that?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: I went to the army in 1968.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what branch or what type of military work did you do in 1968?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: I was in the unit called the First War Echelon or the 20th Regiment, that is the 20th Gardijski puk or Prvi eselon rata, that’s what it was called. I was in the artillery branch in Valeve, specialized in 76 mm cannons. I was in Tito’s Guard at the time, one of Tito’s soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how long did you serve?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: For 18 months.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: After that, did you continue to serve in the reserve of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: For how long?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Until 1985 or 1986, for some 15 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what rank did you achieve?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: A surgeon [as interpreted] -- first class.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sorry, the transcript says "surgeon" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think it was an interpreter's correction to first class.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, private first class I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you. Now, could you tell the Court, please, how big was your village at Prilepnica, approximately how many houses and how many people?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Our village has around 350, 360 households and about 3.000 inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what was the ethnicity of the people who lived in your village?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Before the war there were these 350, 360 Albanian families that I mentioned. There were also about 30 Roma families and some five or six Serbian families.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, could we show the witness a map, Exhibit P36.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: While that's coming up on your screen, Mr. Shaqiri, I would like to ask you: Were you aware of when the NATO bombing began in 1999?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: From the time that bombing started until you left, sometime in April of 1999, was there any NATO bombing in your village?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: No, there wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, if we could enlarge that map a bit on the area slightly north of Gjilan. One more, please, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, on the monitor can you see your village on that map? And there's a pen there I'll have the usher hand you.

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: This is where it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You can actually draw on the screen. If you draw a circle around your village of Prilepnica.

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And could you draw a circle around the other villages that you covered as the imam. You mentioned them before.

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Yes, Kmetofc, bordering Ropotove. This is where the Albanian Muslim families lived, and then there is Verbica and Kosaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we take a screen shot of that and give it the next IC number, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be marked IC28, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Shaqiri, before -- before the NATO bombing started, had you had any problems or violence in your village?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And before the 6th of April, 1999, had there been any significant presence of either the VJ or Serbian police in your village?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: No, there wasn't any.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I then would like to direct your attention to the 6th of April, 1999. Did you hear or see anything unusual on that day?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: That day I was at my mother's visiting my younger brother. This is where the mosque is. It is about 1 kilometre away from my house. I dined there and at 8.10 I heard gun-fire from all sides in Prilepnica. It struck a lot of fear among us because the village is situated in a canyon. And people started to flee their homes and take to the mountainsides.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What did you do when you heard the gun-fire?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: For the moment I was stunned, and after talking with some of my relatives I decided to go in the direction of the southern part of the village from where the gun-shot was heard. I put on my imam uniform and I was walking on the main road, and after 5 or 600 metres I ran into a soldier who was holding two hostages, Nazim Xhelil, now retiree, and Shelik Shaqiri who was a teacher of physical training. Both of them were being held in the middle of the road. I approached them. That soldier asked -- stopped me and asked me who I was. I introduced myself to him, and then I asked him why do we hear gun-shots? He replied in this way: We have received information that there is KLA presence in the village and that the village has to be emptied in order for us to fight the KLA soldiers. I assured them that there was no KLA presence in the village, but nevertheless he ordered me to tell the population to leave their homes. I went back to the mosque and used the loudspeakers of the minaret.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you for a minute and ask you a few questions to go through this. You say you put on your imam uniform before you went in the direction of the shooting. What -- what does your imam uniform look like?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: It is a similar uniform like the one you are wearing, a long robe, dark robe, and I put on a hat, not the imam's hat, but a white cap.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Usually worn by those who go to Haxh.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you say when you approached the area where you heard the shooting, you saw a soldier who had two men you described by name as hostages at gun-point there. Was it just one soldier?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: There was only this person who was holding the two hostages. A little bit further away where the centre of the village is, there was a group of 10 or 15, 12 or 15 people who fired now and again in the air just to strike fear among the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were this other group soldiers as well?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Yes, yes, they were soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How were they dressed? What kind of uniforms did they have?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Most of them had similar -- the same uniform, one colour uniform SMB olive-green-grey uniform. There were one or two who were wearing camouflage uniform, green and blue uniform, camouflage.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is that green and blue mixed together or some green and some blue?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Green and yellow, lemon yellow. That was prevalent. There were other colours, but these were most striking.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you see any kind of insignia or badges or markings of rank on any of these uniforms?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: No, no, they didn't have any rankings that I saw. The soldier -- this soldier who was holding the two people ransom in a way had a cap - bandanna --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- on his head.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And can you tell us anything about the weapons that these men had?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Usually they carried automatic rifles, Kalashnikovs as they called them. There were other weapons, but most of the weapons that I could see were automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You told us before when you were describing this that you spoke with the soldier who was holding the two men hostage. What language did he speak to you in and you speak to him in?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: In Serbo-Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You speak and understand that language?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In addition to Serbo-Croat and Albanian, do you speak or understand any other languages?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: I understand some Arabic, but I have forgotten a lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when and how did you learn Serbo-Croatian?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: All my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned you spoke to the man who was holding those two prisoners and he indicated that they were looking for KLA in the village. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is he the only one you spoke with?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Yes, for the moment he was the only one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I'm sorry, when I stopped you before, I think you had said that you went to make an announcement to the village. Why did you do that?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: He ordered me to do that, to tell the people to leave the village for them, as they told me, to be able to fight the KLA, as they alleged, which in fact did not exist in the village. So in the midst of fire when I started to tell the people: Attention please, attention please, in the microphone, the Hoxha or the imam of the village is talking to you, all the fire stopped. For them to leave the village and to take to the streets. I repeated this message seven or eight times maybe. The people heard me attentively and left their houses and gathered on both roads of the village, one on the east and one on the western part of the village, because the village is divided in two by the river. On the western part of the village, I went there, too. I was heading the crowd of people going in that direction, in the direction of the west. And then I went back to the same soldier, the one who was holding the two people hostage.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what -- did you speak to him again?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I asked him to talk to the officers who had given this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What officers would those be?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: For the moment I didn't know who they were or who he was, but we walked together with this soldier for some 200 metres and we arrived at the end of the village. And there I met three officers. They were dressed in camouflage uniform like the one I described earlier, and they were carrying only pistols. And their caps, they were carrying them on their shoulder.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you speak with them?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Yes. The first -- the first words we exchanged were -- the soldier was the one who addressed the officers and I am quoting his words.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And Mr. Shaqiri, I see now you appear to have some notes in your hand. Can you tell us what those are?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: It's nothing much to speak of. It's just the order of events as you are asking me, just some points, that is the contact with three officers is one of the note. And then I realised that they were holding 100, 150 citizens hostages. This is something which I learned later.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you --

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: I can leave them aside if you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, that's fine. If at some point in time you think it would be helpful to refer to your notes, that's fine, if you'll just let us know when you're referring to your notes. Okay?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: No problem. I don't need them anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But if at some point in time there comes a need, just let us know and you can have a look and we'll know when you're using those. Now, the three men that you spoke to that you understood were officers, did they have any kind of rank or insignia on their uniforms?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: No. They didn't have ranks. They only had the military belt worn by regular police --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- soldiers and the pistol. Their uniform was camouflage one, as I described earlier, green and yellow camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in what language did you converse with them?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: In Serbo-Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Of the three, was there one who seemed to be in charge?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Yes, the one in the middle.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Had you ever seen any of these men before?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What did they tell you they were there for, if they did?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Initially they threatened me and said that they were going to kill me first -- or rather, they were going to execute me first. And they were trying for the firing coming from the eastern, northern, and western part of the village to claim as if it was coming from the KLA, that the KLA was firing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And were you aware of any KLA in your village or in the -- the immediate area around your village?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: There was never a KLA presence in Anamorave.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And that name that you've just given, it appears on the transcript, I don't recognise. Could you say it again and describe what region it refers to?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: It is the east-southern part of Kosovo. It includes Vitir Gjilan, Kamenica, up to Serbia, namely Bujanovc, Presheve. This is what we call Anamorave. In B/C/S it would be ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you said the commander threatened to kill you. Did he say how you could avoid that happening?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: While the firing was going on, firing from different weapons, they were trying to convince me that this was firing from Skorpion or Chinese-make rifles. And I explained to them in this way. I told them: Look, I'm not an expert in equipment or weapons. There is no KLA presence in our village. And I tried, actually, to warn them not to shoot in that direction because about 500 metres further was the village of Kmetofc where Serbs lived. We were surrounded on all sides by Serb-populated villages. The entire northern part and north-eastern part is covered by Musgova, village on the west is Kuvca, again a Serbian village. In south-west, again another Serbian village, so we are surrounded by seven Serbian villages. This is what I told them: If you continue to shoot in this manner, you will even cause harm to your own population, the Serbian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how far was your village from the border with Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Bujanovc is 30 kilometres far from Gjilan and from my village 35 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, the last part of the previous answer given by the witness was: "And blame it on the Albanians."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So obviously they didn't execute you because you're here with us today. What happened after that discussion?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Later on one of the officers, about 42 or 43 years old, he took me aside and we spoke, only the two of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just before you proceed further, Mr. Shaqiri, I'm confused about a reference here in the transcript to Bujanovc. Can you clarify that for me, Mr. Hannis, how that fits?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We can.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us where the town of village of Bujanovc is located?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is that in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: No, Bujanovc is on the border. It's the first town in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I now understand. Thank you. And I'm sorry to have interrupted you, Mr. Shaqiri. If you can take up where you left off there, and you were telling us about speaking to this one officer who was 42 or 43 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What did the two of you talk about?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: His nickname was Russ. I heard the other officers call him Russ. He was not Russian by origin, but this was just his nickname. So I asked him not to make us move from the village because the population was mainly unemployed and they were tied to their homes. I told him that we had never experienced any problems in the past, so this is what he told me: "I see you're an honourable man. An order has come from Belgrade. People must be moved out of Prilepnica. If you have any wits about you, you should flee to one of the neighbouring villages." So he took me inside his military vehicle, in the Pinzgauer. There was his driver as well. And from there we went together to the place where the population was gathered. With us this officer nicknamed Russ also came. The western part of the village had been plundered. Some people were even beaten. Their documents were seized from them, and one of the co-habitants from the village told me what had happened. The officer asked me: What is this person saying? So I told him what the villager said. The officer then ordered for the documents to be given back to the citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did the soldiers do that?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: They just threw them near a wall. That's where they threw these documents. I went to the place where the population was, and this officer and the soldiers were also there present.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: About how many soldiers were with the officer and you when you went to where the people were gathered?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: It was me, the officer, and the driver in the Pinzgauer, while there -- there was a group of 20 to 30 soldiers. They were scattered into groups, because the population was not moved out from the village entirely, it was stopped on the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were the people stopped on the road, were they in cars? Were they on foot? What were they doing?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: They were in cars and also on foot.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When you had earlier, pursuant to the order you'd been given, gone to the mosque and made an announcement to the people, had you told them where they should go?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What did you tell them?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: I just told the people to come out on the roads, to go together to the southern part of the village on a field because the army was in the village. But the army actually stopped the population on the road inside the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What happened next?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: While I was there present, they took a vehicle from a villager and also another four vehicles from other villagers. I was surprised and looked at the officer because that's how they introduced, they said they were regular army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, who said they were regular army and when did they tell you that?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: When I spoke to these three officers in the beginning, they introduced themselves as follows: Listen, Hoxha, we are a regular army. The bombing has started and we will defend our country at any cost.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, before -- well, now when you're gathered on the road where the soldiers have stopped the people, what happened next? Did anyone stay in the village, return to the village, go somewhere else? What happened?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: While we were on the road, there was the Albanian population and the Roma population. We were all there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How about the -- you mentioned I think a few Serb families in your village. Were they present?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: No. The Serb families were in the beginning of the village, on the western part of the village. A platoon had penetrated the village from that side without even knowing that what population lived there. They nearly killed a Serbian woman who was in her courtyard. She then introduced herself, told them that she was a Serb. They didn't believe her right away. The road coming from the west of the village is about 50 metres away from the place that I was speaking about. After they had taken these vehicles, they were firing in the air and they were actually happy that the vehicles were filled up. So while they were firing in the air, the part of the soldiers that were just near the place where I was started firing, too. Somebody could have just gotten killed, but fortunately or unfortunately there was an iron gate nearby. And while they were firing from an automatic rifle, a Serbian soldier got injured. They administered first aid to him. I was just 2 metres away. I asked the soldier: Who inflicted this injury on you? How come you're wounded? And he just simply answered: By ricochet. So the officer nicknamed Russ and some others took this soldier in the same Pinzgauer and told the other soldiers to withdraw. They set off in the direction of Gjilan and we remained in the village. It was necessary for us to report this to the police or other authority because we didn't want to move Rexhep Medeti and Mr. Bajrami --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there for a minute. You said it was necessary to report because you didn't want to move. Before the soldiers left, had the officers or any of the soldiers given you further instructions on what you were supposed to do after they left?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: I think I mentioned it earlier that the order was for the entire village to move out in the direction of Ferizaj in two hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you say -- you said just before I asked you that question that you didn't want to move. So you sought help or permission from some other authority to not have to do that?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: We tried to establish contact with the police in the town, with the chief of the police, and we also tried to contact a local Serb, Vlado Denic, who was the deputy director of the hospital. And with his mediation we hoped to get somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you a couple questions about that. Do you know who the chief of police was in -- well, in Gjilan, I guess, at that time?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Dragan was the chief of police of the police. He is from Ranilluga, Dragan Peric, namely, who was a very good man and an honourable citizen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: He was a Serb?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the other name you mentioned, the deputy director of the hospital, Vlado Denic, he was a Serb?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Yes, he was a Serb, too, but he was from my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And why did you think he might be able to help you? Was there something about his position as deputy director of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Yes. It was because of his position and we thought that by contacting him we might not move from the village. And even if we didn't manage to contact the chief of the police, we wanted to contact his brother, Bora Denic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How far was Gjilan from your village?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: 6 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When you were given the direction to leave within two hours, were you told anything about what would happen at the end of the deadline if you had not complied?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: They said that the following day at 12.00 they were going to lay mines in the village, that that was their order, and that they were going to mine the dam as well because there is a dam in the village. The order came from above and that it was necessary for them to carry it out. They did not threaten to kill us, no, they didn't do this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who went to town to try and talk to the chief of police or Vlado Denic?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Demush Bajrami and Rexhep Mehmeti, Korolube Deniqi [phoen], his pseudonym was Goxhe [phone]. He was wearing a military uniform, a camouflage one, and carrying a Kalashnikov.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, who was wearing this uniform?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Gorulub Denic, a.k.a. Goce, he was a Serb from my village, who was part of the army that had had began the shooting at 8.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And he had not left with the other -- with the rest of the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: When the other soldiers withdrew, he went to his house.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were there any other Serbs from your village who had on the same uniform as these soldiers and participated with them during that day, or was he the only one?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: It was only him on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was he related to the Vlado Denic who was the deputy director of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Yes, they are part of the same family.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So he was part of the delegation that went to -- to Gjilan to see if you could get some relief from this deadline at --

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How long were they gone, approximately?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: The hospital you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, how long were the men who went to town that -- I think you named three men that went to town to try and get some relief. How long were they gone?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: For half an hour, 20 minutes, half an hour maximum.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did all three of them come back?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: I was with them, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So four of you went to town?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what happened when you got there?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: The military guards who were standing guard duty in front of the hospital did not allow us to go in, but with Goce's help, he told them that we were with him. We managed to go in. We met with Vlado. Vlada was also surprised to hear what had happened, and we actually did not allow him to go back to his office. We took him with us, to help us, and to come with us either to Peric, the chief of the police, or to Bora, his brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, Bora is whose brother?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Vlado's brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And what position did he hold?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Vlada was a member of the military staff in Gjilan.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Vlada was or Bora?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Vlada was in the hospital, deputy director, while his brother, Bora, was a member of the military staff in Gjilan.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And by "military staff," are you referring to the VJ or something else?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Yes, the Yugoslav army was there in our country. There were no other formations at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Did you manage to see the chief of police?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: One of the officers who were in my village, he had seen us while we were in the vehicle on the way to the hospital, and he had followed us. Before we left the hospital yard, this officer with his soldiers encircled us. They had their guns pointed at us. He addressed the -- these persons and said ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And said what?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: "Where are you taking this man?" They meant where were they taking me, why they were holding me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who answered and what did --

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: And to this Redzep replied: We wanted to go to the police to report what had happened -- what has happened in our village. The officer then said: There is no police here, no army. I am everything here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, which officer was this? Was this the one that was nicknamed Russ or one of the other three?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: No, it was another officer, not the Russ.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was he one of the three who had been in your village earlier in the day?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Yes, exactly, one of the three officers who had been in my village. He had a moustache. He was about 50 years old, approximately 1.75 metres tall. Then the officer turned to me and said: Have you got your orders? And I replied: Yes. And he asked: What was the order? And I said to him that we have to move in two hours, at least those who are in the village, while those who are out to their works, they have to leave the village by 12.00 the next day. Then he addressed the other persons and said to them: Do you hear this? Do you hear what he is saying? And then he asked Vlado: Who are you? Vlado introduced himself; he said he was the deputy director of the hospital. And -- I'll execute you on the spot. Vlada is a civilised person and he turned to me and said: Shaqiri, you have to obey the order. We went back to the village --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I -- I don't know what happened. I don't know if it's a mistake or whatever. The witness is going along talking and the translation is going along and if you start looking at 22, line 5, where are you. Vlado introduced himself. He said he was the deputy director of the hospital. And then a different voice, translation comes in and says: I'll execute you on the spot. And then it goes to the other voice and says: Vlada is a civilised person and he turned to me and said. I don't know how it got in the middle there but I don't think it belongs there. I'm not sure the witness even said that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, the witness interjected that in Serbo-Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Shaqiri, then Vlado told you that you needed to obey the order and you went back to the village. That was you and your original group of three that were with you?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Yes, the four of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What happened when you got back to the village?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, before you do that I thought perhaps we should clarify this point. Mr. Shaqiri, did you say at one stage just now that someone made the comment: I'll execute you on the spot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it was the officer who threatened Vlado, the Serbian officer, the one who threatened Vlado in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right, thank you. Does that clarify it, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, it does, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I thought there was a mistake there, there wasn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What happened when you got back to the village?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Again, through the loud-speakers, we announced that we must leave the village by all means, and after we set out to meet on the main road Gjilan-Bujanovc, the place is called Bunar, maybe it will come up again later on. I was heading the column. I didn't go in the direction of Gjilan and Ferizaj, but took the eastern direction, the opposite side, in the direction of Dobercan village and this road passes -- goes to Kamenice and Bujanovc.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. About how many people were in your group or your convoy that left that day?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: At least 3.000 inhabitants, over 400 vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And where was your destination? Where were you leading the group to?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Initially I wanted to go to Kmetofc, past that village. The Albanian and Serb families in Kmetofc are divided by the road. Among the Serbian families living close by to the road there was a regular Serb army, this is where they were deployed in Kmetofc. We had passed there several times and nothing had happened to us, but that day they had planted mines on part of the road and there was a police first and then military guard in that place. The police looked at the convoy of people and didn't do anything, but soldiers, army soldiers, stopped us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What happened when they stopped you, did you speak with them?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Yes. They asked us: Why are you leaving, where we were going. And I replied that we have orders from the army to leave the village. And this convoy of people had fled on the orders of the army. The same person, the same military man, showed surprise and he told me: One hears everything these days. He didn't stop me because -- and ask because I said to him that we had orders. And then we continued our way in Dobercan, that is the last village before you go to Gjilan.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At this first point where you stopped, you described police and military. What kind of uniforms were the men you described as police wearing?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: They were the road -- traffic police, wearing the usual uniform, blue uniform. And they had white ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: They had white -- you were indicating something on your arm --

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: White parts on their arm.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the military --

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: It's a white cloth with a ribbon -- with elastic that they wear on the arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And you described the military that were there. What kind of uniforms were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: The soldiers had olive-green-grey uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, from -- from that point, that check-point I guess, where did you go next?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: We stopped at Dobercan village. They had heard what happened in Prilepnica. I talked with my colleague there, with the Hoxha of the village, Muslim priest of the village, who unfortunately on the 15th of June was killed, by some people in uniforms while they were withdrawing from the place, at a very early age of 38.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Dobercan?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: I did my best to distribute -- to spread out the population in the village. I wanted them to go wherever they could to find shelter at this difficult time, but people didn't want us to break and so we wanted to go together everywhere. But 3.000 people was hard to find shelter for in one place. But I had a strong confidence in me to enter the Serbian territory. In the Albanian-inhabited villages I thought to go to Trnovc.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And where is Trnovc located?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: It is next to Bujanovc.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is that in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: No, no. It is in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did your entire group of 3.000 from your village follow you onward from Dobercan?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: For some 12 or 15, 17 kilometres until we reached the administrative boundary when we entered the Koncul village, but before arriving there at Dhen I Bardhe, the Kamenica police took care of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How did they --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They didn't care of us but they looked after that place that I mentioned. They did the usual -- the routine patrols, stopped cars, tractors, and searched them, the usual police searches.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Where did that happen?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: At the triangle of the road that goes from Gjilan to Bujanovc, and then it turns to Fogosh.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is there a village at that location?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: No. Koromjan village inhabited by Serbs is the closest village to that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could put up an exhibit now, it would be 615, which is the Kosovo atlas, and it would be I believe page number 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Shaqiri, I want to show you a map that I hope will show some of the places you've just been telling us about that you went to when you left your village of the 6th of April. And from this place where the Kamenica police searched you, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: We were stopped there, they stopped us. They asked us, and I answered, as I did to the soldiers in Kmetofc, since in Anamorave in the direction of Dumarovc that was the first convoy of people that was being displaced.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could enlarge the upper half of that map. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Shaqiri, can you see your village on this map, Prilepnica? I don't know what you have on your monitor --

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: I can't see very well. Maybe you should move it a little bit on the right side where Gjilan is. I can see Kmetofc. Here is Prilepnica --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... could you put a 1 --

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Yes, if you can enlarge it, it would be better.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can we enlarge it one more time -- oh, I'm sorry -- yes, can we enlarge it one more time and I'll have him draw again. I realise that we have to start over. And if we can have Prilepnica sort of in the upper left of the enlargement, I think everything else will be on there that we want.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Shaqiri, we're going to try and enlarge our map one more time. And now if you can start again, and if you could draw a circle around your village and put the number 1 in --

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Yes, now it's clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The usher will help you.

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Prilepnica is here, number 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you draw a circle around that for me.

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Number 2 is Kmetofc, here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And then show us the second village you went to or the next village you went to?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Kmetofc, number 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And from there, you said Dobercan?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Dobercan.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you draw a circle around that and put a 3 inside it?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And from Dobercan, where did you go next?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: We went -- we continued our way in the direction of Ranilluga, it's a Serbian village, far from the road, in the direction of Dumarovc [as interpreted]. I can't see it here. Here is Koncul. We came approximately here before going to Bujanovc. We walked some 17 kilometres until here, the place where the road divides to go to Dumarovc, that triangle that I mentioned is not shown here. This is where Dhen I Bardhe is. This is where the regular police was deployed. It used to be there all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you a couple more questions. From Dobercan did you go past the village of Ranilluga?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Yes, we passed that and Koromjan.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you draw a circle around that?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you put the number 4 there?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when you got there, which direction did you go?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: We went in the direction of Koncul to come to Bujanovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, what municipality are Ranilluga and Koromjan in? I see a border there?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: They are in Kamenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And from Koromjan, you went in the direction of Bujanovc?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: The last village of Gjilan commune is Dobercan and then starts Kamenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay and how far did you get? Did you get all the way to Bujanovac?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: No. Before arriving in Kocul some 4 or 5 kilometres away, here, the police, the local police came and went before the convoy and stopped us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Before we go on, can you write a number 5 and write a circle around that location where you say you were stopped and contacted by the police.

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now could we take a screen shot of that and save that as the next IC exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be IC29, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now where were these police from?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: The local police of Kamenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And on this map it looks like the number 5 inside the circle there is on the right side or the east side of another border. Have you left Kamenica municipality at this point?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Yes, and we had left the border of Kosova altogether and entered the Serbian territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So what did the Kamenica police tell you when they stopped you at this location?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: I introduced myself to them, telling them that I was imam of the mosque. Three policemen came up front. One of them approached my car and said: We have taken orders from Gjilan from the chief of the police for us to go back to our own homes, because no harm will come to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So what did you and your group of villagers from Prilepnica do then?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: I felt good to hear such words, and I informed my people, telling them to pass the news to all the convoy and return to our homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How long did it take you to get back?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: A very small number of people returned to the village that night. The police in Gjilan and Kamenica had taken positions at crossroads, whereas I stayed in Dobercan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hannis, are you saying that this place called Kamenica is number 5?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Kamenica is a municipality. The police from Kamenica municipality --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- reached them at this location inside Serbia proper and told them that they had orders for them to return.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So -- I've got a mark in front of -- on the plan here that's got a 4 inside it, and then it would appear to be changed to a 5. Is that where we are at the moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's where we are. That's the place where he's indicated they were stopped on their way to Bujanovac and told to turn around. I understood 4 to be in the circle near the name Kormojan. Does that assist Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you're saying the account is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Koromjan is a Serbian village but is not close to the road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This account is that the police from the municipality of Kamenica have entered Serbia and told them to turn back?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's what his testimony is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is that correct, Mr. Shaqiri?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you said you stayed the night where?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: In Dobercan village.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was it just you alone or others from your village?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: People went to many villages because people went to their relatives, acquaintances they had. I went to a friend of mine with some 15 members of my family. That friend of mine is of Turkish nationality.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you return to Prilepnica?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: I did in the evening of the 7th of April, it was a Wednesday, around 6.00 in the afternoon, 1800.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Was it just you and your family or others from the village?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: About 70, 80 per cent of its inhabitants had already returned; the remainder had not yet returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When you got back on the 7th of April, did you notice anything different about the village from when you had left on the 6th?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Our houses had been looted and raided, especially in the western part of the village. Not the entire village was looted. The eastern partly was left intact.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to talk with any of the villagers who had stayed behind on the 6th?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were they able to tell you anything about how this had happened, about how the looting had occurred or about who had done it?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: It had occurred on that day, and in the evening many families had rallied together and they spent the night together. Some houses, especially at the end of the village or in my house was -- and where those 150 people were kept prisoners, were destroyed more or were looted more.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did they tell you who had done it?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: We all knew who did it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, you were on the road in the convoy several kilometres away. What did they tell you about who had done it? Had they seen it happen themselves, the people who remained in your village?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Just an explanation. The entire population left the village. The village was completely deserted. There was not a single Albanian left in it. When some families first returned in the evening of the 6th of April, they found the damage that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So they didn't actually see who had done the damage; it had already occurred by the time they got back. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: No, they didn't see it. You are -- that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps this would be a good time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, it would be, Mr. Hannis. We have a long way to go yet with this witness, have we?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have estimated two and a half hours with his testimony. I've done an hour and a half. I think I'll be two and a half hours total.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Very good. We'll resume at 5.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Shaqiri, we finished talking about the trip you and your fellow villagers made on the 6th of April, and you told us how you returned on the 7th. Did there come a second time when you and the other villagers had to leave Prilepnica?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When was that, what day was that?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: This was on the 14th of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Before I ask you the details about that second trip, can you tell us what -- what did you do in your village during that week after you returned? Was it the normal life you had before the 6th of April?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: No, the life was no longer normal. Every citizen tried his or her best to contact people with authority who were of Serb nationality to avoid moving out from the village because there was no reason for us to move. Subsequently, on the 9th and 10th of April, we stood guard duty together with the police from the town. But this did not last long, and on the 13th of April, while I was getting ready to go to the mosque, around 12.00, 12.30 in the yard of my mother's house, two officers came. They were wearing uniforms, military uniforms, and my brother's wife, my sister- in-law, she got scared and she immediately came back to the house and said to us that there was some soldiers in the yard. I went out in the yard. I met with these soldiers. I knew very well who they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How did you know who they were?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: I knew them from earlier, from before. Ljuba Palamarevic, he worked for a long time in Anamorave region, and not only me but hundreds of other people from my area know him, while Djilas Mladenovic who at that time worked as a director at the radiator factory, I and other citizens knew him as well because we worked in that factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Where is the radiator factory located?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: In Gjilan.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And where did Ljuba Palamarevic work?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: He used to be a lawyer in Binacka Morava and just recently he had taken up the position of a judge at the local court in Gjilan. And that's why the contacts that I and other villagers had with him were very frequent. We were friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What kind of uniforms were these two men wearing on this day, the 13th of April?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Those who came in the yard on the 13th of April were wearing camouflage uniforms, yellow-green camouflage uniforms. I did not notice any military ranks on their uniforms, and they were not armed. They conveyed the order to me and said -- of course they greeted me first, and I will quote now. "Good afternoon, sir." I said: Good afternoon. I asked him: What do you want? And they said that they were looking for the Hoxha, for the imam. Despite the fact that they knew me very well and that I knew them, too, they just wanted to verify my identity. I smiled and said to them: Well, you know that I am the Hoxha here. You could see kind of a happiness on their faces, and they said: It's good for us that we found you. We apologise, but an order has come from the supreme staff in Belgrade, Prilepnica must be evacuated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did he tell you why?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Of course. And I asked him: Why? And he said: We are an army. We have to carry out our orders and we do carry out our orders and we don't know the reasons for those orders. They wanted to leave, but I insisted on them staying for a while because I wanted other people from the village to hear of this. I explained to them that it wasn't easy for someone to tell his people to leave. My youngest son was there in the yard, my nephew, too, my brother's son. So I ordered them to go outside in the road, and whoever they see there, they should invite them in the yard of my house so that they could be informed about the order that was conveyed to me by these officers. Rexhep Mehmeti came, Demush Bajrami followed, and in the meantime Ramadan Mehmeti came there as well. The last who arrived there was a driver at this radiator factory, Reshat Rahmani and when he saw his director he said to him and I'll quote: "Hello director." And the director replied: Hello Reshi. And Reshi said to him: What is this all about? And the director replied: We don't know Reshi. We received the order for Prilepnica to move out. And then Reshi asked him: Where is this taking us then?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What did he say?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: An army is an army, an order is an order. We respect orders, we obey orders, and Prilepnica should be emptied by 9.00 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Shaqiri, did you tell them that you had been ordered to leave and had actually left a week before?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Yes, of course. This is why other villagers, for example, Ramadan, told him: Well, you made us move out from the village once. Why did you make us come back? And Djilas replied: On 6th of April, you were moved out by the paramilitary army. This is what Djilas said. And now he continued: We are dealing with the regular army. And it is Hoxha's mistake because he did not set off in the direction pursuant to the order that was issued to him; he went to an opposite direction. And my reply to this was that I went towards this direction because I knew that road and I cannot go somewhere where I don't feel safe. So there we were told that we should set off in the direction of Ferizaj --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me stop you there for a minute. So when he was talking about that Hoxha had made a mistake before, that meant you; correct?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Yes, that meant me because on the 6th of April I set off with my people in the direction of Bujanovc because it was a free zone, and it was easier for us to walk in this direction because there was no danger involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So on the 6th you had taken your people and gone toward Serbia proper, correct?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And on the 6th where had you been told you were supposed to go, what direction?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: In the direction of Ferizaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, on this day you were also told that this was the regular army doing it, as opposed to the paramilitary army that had ordered you out on the 6th. What did you understand the term "regular army" to mean in this context?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: I always have respected the regular army. As every other country in the world who respects its own army, we as well did not have any problems whatsoever with the army --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just hold on there, Mr. Shaqiri. You've obviously misunderstood that question. I think Mr. Hannis should explain it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What did you understand the difference to be between the regular army and the paramilitary army that had been there the week before?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: For me there was no difference. They were wearing the same uniform. It didn't even occur to me to call them paramilitary army. This is what Djilas called them, this formation of the 6th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you a question about Djilas and Ljuba Palmarevic, you indicated one was a director at the factory?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Ljuba --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And one was a lawyer who became a judge?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Djilas was the director of the radiator factory, while Ljuba, he had worked in another cooperative in Binicka Morave and he had become a judge, he was a judge then.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So I take it these two men are not professional soldiers or career soldiers of the VJ?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So when they're in uniform there that day, what army are they a part of, if you know?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Serbian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But not -- not the regular full-time army?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: No, no. Reserve officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were there any other soldiers with them when they came to the village on the 13th?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: As villagers were coming in to my yard, the third soldier came in as well and he brought three weapons with him, three Kalashnikovs. He distributed one to each, one to Ljuba, one to Palamarevic. We sat down and we had a conversation. It was a heated conversation because we refused to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what was their response to your refusal to leave?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: In order for me to be able to obey their order, I requested an escort, and one of them then asked me what kind of escort I wanted, a police or a military escort. And I said to him: It's all the same for me. I just don't want to take all the responsibility. It doesn't matter whether it will be the police or the army who will escort us. So I will now quote what I actually said to them. My regards to your staff. I demand an escort. If you promise an escort, then I will organise the move out; and if you don't, then I will not organise the moving out of the villagers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did they agree to provide an escort?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: They agreed to convey my demand to the staff, and they said that they will -- they would inform me of their answer. They left then, the three of them. Shortly after, three villagers, Demush, Rexhep, and another person, Ramadan Rrama, respectively, they went to the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: In Gjilan. And they informed me that they had spoken with the police. They had given me even a name of the policeman, but I don't remember it. And the police had asked them who had issued that order. And they told them that it was Ljuba and Djilas. This is what they said to me. These are their words. They actually said that the policemen told them that the army had taken the situation into their hands and that the police could no longer do anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So that's what Demush, Rexhep, and Ramadan reported to you when they returned?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Yes, Ramadan, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So when -- when -- when Ljuba and Djilas had told you that you were going to have to leave again, did they tell you -- did they give you a deadline?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: The deadline was for us to go out at 9.00 to the point, to -- on the main road, and within an hour, Ljuba and Djilas, they both returned to Prelepnica. They didn't meet me when they returned. They simply left a message for me, and it contained just a small change, to be at the well at 8.00 and that an escort was approved.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So after you had learned of what the police had to say about this and you got this message from Ljuba and Djilas changing the time from 9.00 to 8.00, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Well, we prepared ourselves that night. People were crying. They were crying more than it rained. And the following day at 7.30, the whole population of the village was on the road, in tractors, motor cultivators, cars.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how many people in your convoy this time, the same as the week before?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: The same as the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was there an escort waiting for you that morning?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: On the 13th of April, the army encircled the village because some villagers began to fled -- to flee.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now that they came, nobody could leave the village any longer. In the end of the village an APC, almost the same one as the one on the 6th of April manned by the three officers, was positioned at 2 kilometres from the main road, at the end part of our village. I approached them. I greeted them, and they asked me, I quote: "Hoxha, have you got it all in place? Do you need a bus or some fuel?" And I said to them: No, I don't need anything. I just need the escort that you promised. So then they said to me: You can go now and the escort is waiting for you at the well. On the way to the well, there is the village of Kosac, and people from this village were also ordered to leave. And I was actually surprised to see them there and to see them joining our convoy -- Q. Approximately how many people were in that group from that village?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: I don't know how many there were. Maybe 300, 400, up to 600. I would say 3 to 400.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did they all join you?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: They joined the convoy from my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I need to back up just a second. I forgot to ask you. You mentioned seeing the three officers, and I take it that's Ljuba Palamarevic and Djilas from the battery factory. Who was the third one?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Their driver. I don't know his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is he the same man that you referred to earlier as having brought the weapons that had been given to them on the day before?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the same. He worked in the people's defence in Gjilan.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: After the villagers from Kosac joined your convoy, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: We walked for another 50 or 60 metres to the main road. There we stopped. A reservist offended me, said to me: Why did you stop here? And I said to him: I have to wait for the escort. And he said: Wow, you want an escort? He threatened me, but I was determined to wait there. It was ten past 8.00. I want to mention a small detail here. A black Mercedes came there. It belonged to high-ranking officers. There were four persons in that Mercedes. I would say all of them were generals. They stopped the Mercedes. I was 5 or 6 metres far from this vehicle speaking to this reservist, military person. They continued towards Gjilan, and the military person contacted the military staff in Gjilan via radio. The same question that was put to me by Ljuba at the turn, whether I needed a bus or not or whether I needed some fuel, the same question was put by the people from the staff. And I gave the same answer. I said I didn't need any. And then they just replied: Let them wait there. The escort will be there in five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Shaqiri, when you left that morning on the 14th, what was your ultimate destination? Had you been told to go to a particular location?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: I didn't know. They just told us to go in the direction of Ferizaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the Serbian name for Ferizaj is Urosevac?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you mentioned this reservist who offended you at this first crossroads. When you say "reservist," what -- what organisation are you talking about? He was a reservist in what?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: He was a reservist in the police force. He was wearing a dark blue uniform, a winter uniform, that is heavy clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how did you know he was a reservist as opposed to a regular policeman?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Because I used to wear the same uniform for 15 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. When you were in the army reserve or the police reserve?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: In the army reserve.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is there any other factor that helped you distinguish what you sometimes refer to as the regular army and army reserve or regular policeman and police reserve, as far as the appearance of those individuals?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: I want to make an explanation. During the time I was a reservist - and I have seen other people doing the same - we kept the uniforms at home to be ready when they might call us for some exercises. At the time there were both uniforms, military police and the usual army. They used the same uniforms, that is, the military police. My brother had the same police uniform; he was a reservist.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Any differences, generally speaking, in physical appearance between reservist and full-time police or army personnel in terms of conditioning or age?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: I may distinguish two aspects. The regular army soldiers always obeyed military commands. They went in large formations, not in small formations of one or two, whereas people of various ages above 35 or 40, they always acted in groups without having any kind of certain command, at least this is what I thought, this is my impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Shaqiri, I want to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm -- sorry, Mr. Hannis, to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I have to say I don't understand the comparison of the uniforms at all. Mr. Shaqiri, why did you mention military police uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For many years on end, we used to keep a uniform at home at a reservist. And now and again when there was some mobilisations for military exercises or drilling, we reservists participated in these exercises organised by the regular army. And the army always supplied us with uniform -- with SMB uniform, that is green uniform, one plain uniform, and dark green uniform to other units, but we acted together in military barracks. That was in the context of a unified military command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What do you mean by military police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By this I mean a unit belonging to the regular army or unit belonging to the reserve army. It was a military unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And did it have any particular duties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Depending on the orders we were given by the army, whatever exercises were organised we abided by the orders given to us, but nothing specific.
