utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I've simply managed to increase my confusion, Mr. Hannis. I don't understand what's being said about -- it may be me alone. I don't understand what's being said about uniforms. If you want to clarify, please do, if you don't feel it's necessary, then carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to try one other question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Shaqiri, were there any differences between the uniforms of the regular army, regular full-time VJ, and the uniforms that the army reservist wore, any difference in terms of colour, quality of uniforms, texture, anything like that that you could tell by looking at a uniform and saying: That's a reservist uniform, that's a regular army uniform?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Someone at the age of 40 or 50 that wears a winter uniform in summer, because this is what we kept at home, and the young man of 20 -- you can tell between those two categories of people. I said earlier that the soldiers didn't come to our homes. I don't -- I can't speak for other places because the soldiers went in columns under commands, whereas these people acted in groups of two or three using private cars. The regular soldier didn't have any private car, whereas these people had and they looted and raided our homes and took away the goods from our homes in their cars. This is the difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I'll --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This arose, Mr. Shaqiri, because you said that you recognised a police reservist uniform because you had worn one for 15 years. And we understood that you were an army reservist, and therefore we're confused - at least I am - about the relationship between an army reservists uniform and a police reservist uniform.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The blue uniforms were worn also by the aviation army -- Yugoslav air force --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, do without anymore complications. Just confine yourself to the two examples I've given you. So tell us if they are -- if there is a difference between a police reservist uniform and an army reservist uniform.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The military uniform had a green, olive-green-grey colour, dark green, whereas the military police uniform usually wore light blue uniform or blue uniform, at least this is how it was in my time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So why would you then say that you recognised the uniform of a police reservist, which is blue, because you had for 15 years been wearing the same uniform, but as an army reservist we would expect you to have a green one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, mine was green, that is true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. It's obviously me. I'll go back to you, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Shaqiri, I want to move on to your journey on that day. Where did you eventually end up at the end of -- of your travels after you left your village on the 14th?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: It is true that after five minutes, Mila came. A road traffic -- normal road traffic policeman. He said that: I am the one who will escort you by a police car.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there for a second. I want to work -- I want to jump forward and then come backwards and we'll go through your journey step by step. But what was your ultimate destination? Where was the final place you had ended after you left your village on that day?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: We ended in Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And what town in Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: I was in Senakos of Gostivar with 925 inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And approximately how long did it take you to make the journey from your village to Macedonia in number of hours or days?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: It took us one day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And during that --

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Until the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. During that journey to the border with Macedonia, did you go through a number of check-points?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And we'll talk about each one in a minute, but in general who was manning the check-points that you went through, was it civilians, army, police, paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: At Kllokot check-point, I saw people wearing the same uniform as the policeman I mentioned, that is blue uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you from your village, did you go to -- did you go to Gjilan this time, to the town of Gjilan?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Yes. Mila escort us up to Livos.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And Mila was the local policeman from where?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: He is from Ranilluga, a regular police, road -- traffic police.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was he the only person in your escort or were there other policemen?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: He was the only one up to Livos. There -- we stopped there and we saw a bus in front of us and we saw the last inhabitants of Livos getting on that bus. In the meantime, another bus from Zhegra came and until Partizani road as we call it, which goes in the direction of Tetova, the buses came with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if we could put up a map, this again will be the Kosovo atlas 615, at page 24 in the e-court version.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to take you from Gjilan to Macedonia, Mr. Shaqiri, and you'll have a map on your screen in a moment that I hope shows most of the route that you went on and we'll see if it's big enough. From Gjilan, what was the next village or town you went through?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Parteshi --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can we enlarge that a couple of steps -- or can we reduce it one or two steps? Okay. Let's try that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: From Gjilan you went to Parteshi?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: First lower Livos, then Partesh.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Can you use the pen. Again I'll have the usher hand it to you.

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And can you draw a circle and put a number 1 around Partesh.

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: From Partesh, where did you go next?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Here, Radivojce.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And after that what was the next village?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Kllokot.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see the road divides there and it appears that one road goes south towards Vitia or Vitina --

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And one goes west to Ferizaj. Could you draw a circle around it and put 2?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: We went to the village of Viti.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you draw a circle around Kllokot and put a 2 there.

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And why did you decide to go to Viti instead of Ferizaj?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: At Livos the escort was changed. Now we have a white Zastava car, 101, Jovak, also a traffic police officer in Gjilan, with three other policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So a total of four policemen are escorting you now?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Yes. Now we have a total of four policemen, and we followed them wherever they went.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And they took you in the direction of Viti at that crossroads?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Where did you go after Kllokot?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: We passed through Viti.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And from Viti, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: We went to the main road that goes to Ferizaj and Skopije, the main road.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you draw a circle with the number 3 in it around Viti.

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And from there, where did you go next? .

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: There is a village here, maybe I need to consult my notes about the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, if you -- if you want.

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Yes, we went to Duganaj, this is the name of the village we went to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And where is that located, approximately, if you don't see it on the map?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Duganaj is situated some 15 kilometres before you enter the Macedonian border. I can't read it here in this map. I can't see it very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I -- if you look directly south of Ferizaj, toward the bottom of the map, I see something that appears to have a name like the one you're describing to me. It looks like Duganovic or Duganaj.

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It must be this, it reads Duganaj. It's along the main road where it divides with Partizani road, it goes towards Tutova. Yes, that's it, Duganaj, now I see it. It goes in the direction of Tutova or Prizren, it divides here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you draw a circle around it and put the number 4 if you see it now.

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And from there where did you go?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: The road continues towards Gllobocika or Macedonia, Jazhince is the first village in the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And that would be south of what you can see on the map here?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Yes, it is at the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could take a screen shot of that and give it the next IC number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be IC30, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And then to complete the journey, if we could put up another page from the Kosovo atlas and I think that would be page 28.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Shaqiri, were you familiar with this route that you were taking, had you ever been along that route before?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: I passed quite rarely.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if on this map we could enlarge the upper half. One more time, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In the upper left-hand corner, I don't know if you can see the name, it's the village that you just told me about before called --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we enlarge it one more time. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Gllobocika is where we went here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And is that where you crossed the border into Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Had you been in this part of Kosovo before?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: I don't think I have used this road because usually I went through Skopije.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: During your journey on the 14th of April from Gjilan to the Macedonian border, did you notice anything about the villages you were passing through on the way?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: The Albanian villages like Livos was vacated of its people. Budrika didn't have a single inhabitant. In Radivojce, which I encircled, there was only an old man and an old woman crying. I didn't see other people. There we saw Serbian army vehicles that were covered with hay between two houses, camouflaged. We saw barbed wire on the road, we had to come around it. And they insulted us, and -- but we never stopped. For some -- after some 5 or 6 kilometre at a water tap, there was a check-point and it was an army check-point. They were wearing olive-green uniforms. In Duganaj we waited for three hours in the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you: When were you across the border into Macedonia, were there any check-points or border guards or police or army?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Before we arrived at the border, it was some 5 or 6 kilometres away from the border, that was a military check-point. The officer stopped us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What happened when he stopped you, did you talk with him?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Yes. I introduced myself to him and informed him where our convoy was heading to and that we were being escorted by police. He asked me where the police was, and I told him that they went back to make sure that the convoy was all in order because we were approaching the border. He ordered me to go and line up people in their cars, 50 by 50, for us to go to the border. But initially he said that he would search them to see if they were carrying any weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And this person, was he a soldier or a policeman?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: He was an army is officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What kind of uniform was he wearing?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: The green uniform, olive-green.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Camouflage or solid colour?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Solid green-grey uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did he have any rank or insignia that you recall?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: I didn't recall seeing any.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What did -- what, if anything, did you say to him when he said they were going to search your convoy?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: I assured him that nobody was carrying any weapons, but of course it was his right to check, to make sure, and that I obeyed the order he gave me. I left my car and walked, informing everyone in the convoy that they would be searching them for weapons. I couldn't make all -- I couldn't make it up to the end of the convoy. After informing 50 or 60 cars, vehicles, I gave order for them to pass the news to everyone. By the time I returned to the head of the column Jova arrived, and he asked me in Albanian because he speaks Albanian very well like me: Why did you stop, he said?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And Jova is the policeman with the other three escorting you?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Yes. And I told him that the military check-point stopped us and that they wanted to search us for weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: He laughed and said that nobody has weapons, but I think we -- he said: Maybe you want to -- they want you to go back to Kacanik because it is not allowed at this place to cross the border. It's not allowed to cross the border at this check-point. If you want to cross the border at this place and if you agree, then maybe you have to pay them money. I agreed. I didn't care how much it would cost us because there was no way we could go back. And I walked for some 10 or 15 metres; before my car there was a soldier. When I approached him he asked me, and I am quoting: "Is this your car?" I said: Yes. Without any reason, he hit me with his weapon on my stomach. I bent a little. For the second time he hit me on my leg and I was suffering from my leg for a long time. Then he started to slap me until I kind of woke up because for some moments I kind of lost consciousness. My mother was sitting on the front seat and near the place where the soldier was hitting me was my younger son and then my wife. And on the back seat was my sister-in-law with her younger son. And then my people was following behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What happened then after this soldier hit you?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Someone informed Jova that: The Hoxha is being beaten, and he intervened.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What happened after Jova intervened, what happened to the soldier who had hit you?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I -- at that moment I was unable to hear well. I had a noise on my -- in my ear, but other people told me that Jova shouted - and I'm quoting - "Don't hit the man." And the officer and Jova pulled that soldier away from me. Jova stayed with the soldier while the policeman returned to me and apologised, and I am quoting --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you. You said Jova stayed with the soldier and the policeman returned. Did you mean the policeman or the officer?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Not the policeman, but the officer who had issued the order to line up the vehicles 50 by 50 while the traffic policeman, he remained there with the soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And this officer is the first one you had talked to when you stopped there, the same one?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Yes, the one I had spoken to shortly before.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: He apologised to you, and then what happened?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Yes. Then he was trying to convince me that he was innocent, and I quote: "Please believe me, Hoxha, that it's not my fault." I lost control for a moment, and in a strict voice I told him: You are not innocent. It is your fault because this is your soldier, and it's not a civilised thing to beat up a Hoxha in the presence of his own family and in the presence of his own people. But the officer then in return just promised that he will let my column and my people go through the border without being searched. I said to him that I will pray to God for his sins in case he lets all the villagers from my village pass the border safely. He kept his word and I kept mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And once you got across the border, where did you and your group go to stay that first night?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Before we crossed the border, this soldier, this officer, handed us over to the border police. There is a border station there, so he handed us over to the person in charge of the border station. He ordered us to leave all our vehicles in a field nearby and to leave the car keys inside as well as the licenses of our vehicles. All of you leave your keys and your licenses. Maybe you will find them when you come back. This is what happened. After that, we crossed the border on foot, all of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you ever get to go back and get your vehicles and your licenses?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: The -- we spent the first night in the zone between the two borders and the next day in the evening, sometime after 7.00 p.m., buses from Macedonia took us to different camps. As I mentioned earlier, I was in Senakov village together with 925 villagers from my village. Others went to the camp called Stenkovac 1. Some went to other camps, and according to some statistics we were all scattered in 24 states throughout the world. When we returned, some earlier and some later, we didn't find anything. We didn't find our vehicles. Those that had remained had been burned and looted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When did you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I be clear who it was who told you to leave the vehicles in the field?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The chief of the customs police. I think he was from Viti. He was about 60 years old.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Shaqiri, when you -- when did you return to your village after the war then?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: I returned on the 25th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we show you Exhibit P1798, 1798, which is a photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you notice any damage in your village that was not there when you left on the 13th or 14th of April?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: We found the village completely burnt, destroyed, looted. The mosque burnt.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recognise that photograph that's on your screen now?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: This is another photograph. This is not the mosque in my village. It must be a mosque from another village.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You don't recognise this particular one?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, when --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you again, Mr. Hannis, just to be clear. Mr. Shaqiri, did you mean to say it was the chief of the customs police who told you to leave the vehicles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And is that something distinct from the border police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The border police and the chief of the police, they were one thing. I could not add anything to this. He was wearing a police uniform, a blue uniform. He introduced himself, and he ordered us to leave the vehicles in the field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you notice any difference between his police uniform and what you recognised as a regular police uniform? Was it a solid colour or camouflage?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: It was a solid colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we show the witness Exhibit P24, please.Q. Mr. Shaqiri, why did you and your fellow villagers leave Kosovo on the 14th of April, 1999?A. Simply because of the order and the fact that our village was encircled by the army at that time, on the 13th of April. There was no other way out for us except to fulfil -- to obey these orders or to fight. Since we were not able to fight, we just obeyed their orders as calmly as possible.Q. Were you afraid of NATO bombing? A. No.Q. Were there any significant battles or fighting between the KLA and Serbian police or VJ in your village or the immediate area that you know of?A. Nowhere, not in my village or in Anamorava.Q. Could you have a look at the map that's on your screen now and tell us, can you recognise or can you point out to the Judges the general route you took from your village to Macedonia? A. From Prilepnica, we went to Gjilan. We passed by Cernice, Gladove, Zhegra, Kllokot, and we returned through the road from Sllatine to Viti, then we came on this road leading to Dubrava. And finally to Gllobocika.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we take a screen shot of that and give it the next IC number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be IC31, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Shaqiri, when you were in Macedonia, do you recall, were you interviewed by any representatives of the OSCE or some other human rights organisation about how you came to leave Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we put Exhibit 2288 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That last exhibit, Mr. Hannis, the witness seemed to have marked in part. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: As he went along.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And it would really be absolutely impossible to tell what he marked on it because it already has markings in the same colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think if you use the exhibit in conjunction of the transcript where he said we went from here to here to here you could follow on the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I take your point it's not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I just wondered if it's even necessary since we've had the route actually drawn for us already. But anyway, the point is --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I was trying to identify his particular route. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Shaqiri, what's your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: 6th March 1949.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And are you the only imam from Prilepnica?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is there -- do you know any other Shaqiri who has a first name Abylthaqin A-b-y-l-t-h-a-q-i-n?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Does this document refer to you? I know it's in English -- oh, maybe it's not on your screen yet?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That appears to refer to you, even though the first name is misspelled?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Yes. My name is misspelled. There is a letter missing, a D, A- b-d and it's not T, it should be H, Haqim. So it's A-b-y-d --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. After the interview, did anybody read back the information they'd taken from you or did you sign anything?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I asked you multiple questions, so now I don't know which one you're answering yes. Did they read it back to you?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you sign it?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Yes, I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't have any more questions about that document, and I don't have any more questions for you at this time. I think Defence counsel may have some questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you help me, is the document signed?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is not. This is from our database. This is not the raw form that would have been used with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we'll proceed in this order: General Pavkovic, General Lazarevic, Mr. Sainovic, Mr. Milutinovic, General Lukic, and General Ojdanic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's very little I can do with ten minutes that I might not have to almost repeat tomorrow in terms of a set up, but if you would like me to go ahead, I certainly will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, I would like you to, please, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Shaqiri, my name is John Ackerman. I represent General Pavkovic, along with Aleksander Aleksic and our case manager Aleksander Vujic. I'm going to have quite a few questions to ask you, as it turns out, and I'm going to try to make those questions as -- as easy to understand as I possibly can. If you don't understand a question that I ask you, please let me know that you don't understand it and I will rephrase it so that you understand exactly what I'm asking. Would that be a fair thing to do?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Everything is all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Just as a kind of preliminary, basic question, would I be safe in assuming that you're like most of us, that your memory tends to fade with the passage of time?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Some things do fade; that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I notice that you've even brought some notes here with you today just in case you had some difficulty remembering something; correct?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter could not hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think he said "po," Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you have given your account of these events, either completely or incompletely, on a number of occasions, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And for instance, you just saw on the screen one of the occasions where you gave an account of what happened, and I think -- I think this occasion when you were interviewed in Macedonia, that was like on the 19th of April as I recall, just basically right after you had arrived there. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And of course that would have been a time when your memory probably would have been extremely clear about the things that had happened to you over the last couple, three days?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Now -- then the next time that I'm aware of that you talked about these events was about six days later on the 25th of April, 1999, when you talked to Kathrine Driguet [phoen], do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Yes, in French.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, that was in French, and of course there was an interpreter there interpreting into your language, into Albanian, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: It was very difficult because the interpreter was not a good one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: After this interview had been completed, the interpreter certainly read to you the statement and gave you a chance to make any corrections that you would want to make. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And it was read to you in a way where you can understand what that interpreter was telling you. Isn't that true? It wasn't read hastily, it was read carefully, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: At normal speed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And after it had been read to you and you had heard what the interpreter told you that was in the statement, you then signed at the end what's called a witness acknowledgement; correct?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that acknowledgement has this language, which is a little different from normal, it says: "I declare upon my honour and conscience that the information contained in this statement, which has been read over to me in my language, accurately reflects the interview held on 25 April 1999." Do you remember signing that?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you ever read the certification that was signed by the interpreter?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. And you understood that when you signed this and acknowledged this, that what you were saying was the things you had said in this statement were true to the best of your recollection; correct?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The next time then that -- that I know that you gave a statement was in 2001, in June of 2001, on the 19th and the 22nd, to Annette Murtagh an interviewer from this Tribunal. Do you remember that statement?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And again, once you had finished giving that statement, it was typed up into English and read to you by the interpreter, and you were given an opportunity to make any additions or corrections that you believed necessary, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And just to underscore that, you were asked to sign the bottom of each page after it was read to you, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Yes, I signed, I know I signed, but I don't know if it is on every page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would you take my word for it or do you want me to have it shown to you?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: I take your word for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. The witness acknowledgement on that one says: "This statement consisting of eight pages has been read over to me in the Albanian language and is true to the best of my knowledge and recollection." And you signed that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that was about two years after the events that you've testified about today - correct - 2001?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The next time that you were asked to make any kind of a statement about this matter was on the 5th of February, 2002. You gave a statement to a Jan Pfundheller. Do you remember giving that statement?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: I know that I have corrected some technical mistakes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, that's the one I'm referring to. And again, you signed that one, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Having corrected it, yes, I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, and what -- what you said there was also true to the best of your knowledge and belief; correct?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: These were just mistakes like the date, my birth date, the name of my father, and some other mistakes. So those that I noticed, I corrected them and I underlined them and then initialled them. So I corrected technical mistakes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that, and we'll get into those in a little more detail when we talk tomorrow. One more quick question: You then provided some information to the Prosecutor's office after you arrived here on 28 August when you talked to attorneys Keith Scully and Irina Dragulev and gave some supplemental information about these events, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Yes, photographs and --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, and you were also telling them the truth when you -- when you told them those things. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: I told them the other part after I returned to Kosova. The filming and the photographs that I had taken of the burnt mosques and the house and some other photographs of my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: My question was: You were telling them the truth when you told them the things you told them on the 28th, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that's a good place to stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's very helpful, Mr. Ackerman. Just one thing perhaps you could clarify. The interview you mentioned with Pfundheller, what organisation or group --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: ICTY, Your Honour, OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's another OTP?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, Mr. Shaqiri, we need to adjourn there for today and resume your evidence tomorrow; that will be at 2.15. You need to be back here in place to continue giving evidence at 2.15 tomorrow. Meanwhile, it is extremely important that you do not discuss any part of your evidence with anyone, and by that I mean either the evidence you've already given or the evidence you may yet give in the case. You can talk about anything else you wish with anyone you see, but you must not, with anyone, discuss any aspect of your evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your advice, Your Honour, and I will respect it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. And we'll resume tomorrow at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 6th day of September, 2006, at 2.15 p.m. 23 24
